lines.speaker: sarah
lines.text: For your Order Fulfillment Service, how did you design the retry and dead-letter logic using Celery and Redis to handle peak traffic?

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Well, you know, when I was working on that order-processing microservice over a three-month internship with a team of four other developers, we had this massive issue with cron jobs just timing out during peak traffic, so I personally rewrote the whole queueing system in Celery and Redis by adding an exponential backoff decorator to the task definitions that pushed failed jobs to a Redis-backed dead-letter queue after three attempts, which totally saved us because when peak season hit, we handled double the normal traffic and I managed to cut the average processing latency all the way down from 40 seconds to 3 seconds flat, which reminds me of the coffee machine we had in the break room that also used to break down all the time.

lines.speaker: sarah
lines.text: Thank you. Moving on. For your Campus Marketplace App, how did you design the database schema to handle growing user traffic?

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: For the Campus Marketplace App, I designed the database schema entirely by myself during a two-month period for a community of over 300 active users, where I set up MongoDB collections for users, listings, and messages with indexing on the item category fields, which honestly reminds me of when I used to organize my entire comic book collection alphabetically by publisher and genre in these big plastic bins that I kept under my bed, but getting back to the database, I made sure the schema could handle rapid queries as new student listings poured in during the start of the semester.
